explanations.explanation: You got it, baker. Esther, the queen, has no summons and walks into that court anyway. The text says that as soon as the king saw her standing there, "she found favor in his sight." (Esther 5:2) Going in unsummoned could mean death (Esther 4:11), so that's a very good moment for a king to be glad to see you.

I get why you'd worry, friend. Esther is standing there uninvited, and going in without being summoned could mean death (Esther 4:11). But the text says that as soon as the king saw Queen Esther standing in the court, "she found favor in his sight." (Esther 5:2) So the moment goes her way, and I can finally unclench my mustache.

That's the one, baker. The king holds out the gold scepter in his hand, and Esther comes forward and touches its tip (Esther 5:2). It's the king's signal that she can come closer. I'd have touched that thing with my whole mustache.

Close to the royal stuff, friend, but not quite. The king doesn't hold out a crown. The text says he extended "the gold scepter in his hand toward Esther," and she touched its tip (Esther 5:2). The crown stays right where it is.

A ring would be a fancy way to do it, baker, but it's not what the text says. The king holds out the gold scepter that's already in his hand, and Esther approaches and touches the tip of it (Esther 5:2). That's the whole moment, one gold scepter and one very careful queen.

Exactly right, baker. The king asks, "What is your request? Even up to half the kingdom, it will be given to you." (Esther 5:3) Half a kingdom! That's the biggest offer anybody ever made over a cookie plate, and I've never even seen a cookie plate come close.

That sounds generous, friend, but the king says something different. He says, "What is your request? Even up to half the kingdom, it will be given to you." (Esther 5:3) No provinces are named, just half the kingdom. The offer is even bigger than the one you picked.

Nice try, baker, but the text doesn't carve out the throne. The king says, "What is your request? Even up to half the kingdom, it will be given to you." (Esther 5:3) That's the limit he names, up to half the kingdom. There's no fine print in what he says.

explanations.answer: The king and Haman at her banquet today
explanations.explanation: You've got it, friend. Esther says, "If it pleases the king, may the king and Haman come today to the banquet I have prepared for the king." (Esther 5:4) Haman is the king's top official, the one who promised money to destroy the Jews (Esther 3:9). The king can give her half a kingdom, and she asks for a dinner guest list.

explanations.answer: An end to the law against the Jews
explanations.explanation: That's a big request, baker, and I can see why you'd pick it. But it's not what Esther asks here. She says, "If it pleases the king, may the king and Haman come today to the banquet I have prepared for the king." (Esther 5:4) Her request is a banquet invitation.

explanations.answer: A pardon for Mordecai at the gate
explanations.explanation: Mordecai, Esther's cousin, is the one who urged her to go to the king (Esther 4:7-8), so I see why he came to mind. But Esther doesn't ask for anything about him here. She says, "If it pleases the king, may the king and Haman come today to the banquet I have prepared for the king." (Esther 5:4) The only thing on her request list is the banquet.

Not quite, friend, because the king does the opposite of slowing down. He says, "Hurry," and commands, "and bring Haman, so we can do as Esther has requested." (Esther 5:5) The king is the one rushing the whole thing along. So the statement on the card is the false one.

That's right, baker. The king doesn't say to take it slow. He says, "Hurry," and commands, "and bring Haman, so we can do as Esther has requested." (Esther 5:5) When a king says "Hurry," I'd be moving faster than a cookie sheet out of a hot oven.

explanations.answer: Come back tomorrow for another banquet
explanations.explanation: That's it, baker. Esther says, "may the king and Haman come tomorrow to the banquet I will prepare for them. Then I will answer the king's question." (Esther 5:8) The king has asked twice, and she still holds her answer for one more day. I think the king's patience is being tested here.

explanations.answer: Let Mordecai join them at the table
explanations.explanation: I see why Mordecai came to mind, friend, since he's Esther's cousin and part of the whole situation. But the text never has her ask for him to join them. She says, "may the king and Haman come tomorrow to the banquet I will prepare for them." (Esther 5:8) Her answer is a second invitation.

explanations.answer: Send Haman away from the palace
explanations.explanation: That would be a quick fix, baker, but it's the opposite of what Esther does. She keeps Haman on the guest list and says, "may the king and Haman come tomorrow to the banquet I will prepare for them." (Esther 5:8) Haman isn't sent anywhere, he's invited back. Then she says she will answer the king's question.

That's right, baker. The text says Mordecai, Esther's cousin, "did not rise or tremble in fear at his presence." (Esther 5:9) Haman was walking out full of joy, and Mordecai just stays put. I think it was a very quiet kind of standoff.

explanations.answer: He bows down to the ground
explanations.explanation: That's not what the text says, friend. Mordecai, Esther's cousin, "did not rise or tremble in fear at his presence." (Esther 5:9) There's no bowing in this verse. If he had bowed, Haman's whole day would have gone differently.

explanations.answer: He gets up and walks away
explanations.explanation: That's a reasonable guess, baker, but the text doesn't have Mordecai moving at all. It says he "did not rise or tremble in fear at his presence." (Esther 5:9) Mordecai is Esther's cousin, and here he doesn't get up. He stays right where he is at the king's gate.

That's it, friend. The text says Haman "was filled with rage toward Mordecai." (Esther 5:9) One minute he's glad of heart, and the next he's full of rage. That's a fast drop, like a cookie sliding off the cooling rack.
That's a kind guess, baker, but pity isn't what Haman feels. The text says he "was filled with rage toward Mordecai." (Esther 5:9) Nothing in the verse shows him feeling sorry for anyone.

Fear is close to the story, friend, since it's in the verse. But it's Mordecai who doesn't tremble in fear, and Haman is the one filled with something else. The text says Haman "was filled with rage toward Mordecai." (Esther 5:9)

I can see why you'd think so, baker, since Haman is full of rage. But the text says, "Nevertheless, Haman restrained himself and went home." (Esther 5:10) He keeps it in and walks away from the gate. So it doesn't come out right there.

That's right, friend. The text says, "Nevertheless, Haman restrained himself and went home." (Esther 5:10) He's full of rage, but he holds it in and leaves the gate. Holding it in is not the same as letting it go, and I think Haman is still carrying it.

explanations.answer: Only he joined the king at Esther's banquet
explanations.explanation: You've got it, baker. Haman tells them, "Queen Esther invited no one but me to join the king at the banquet she prepared, and I am invited back tomorrow along with the king." (Esther 5:12) Haman lists it with his wealth, his sons and his promotions. I think he'd have put it on a banner if he'd had the time.

explanations.answer: The king named him governor of Susa
explanations.explanation: That sounds like a Haman brag, friend, but it's not in the text. He adds, "Queen Esther invited no one but me to join the king at the banquet she prepared, and I am invited back tomorrow along with the king." (Esther 5:12) The title of governor never comes up in the verse.

explanations.answer: Esther asked him for his advice
explanations.explanation: That would be a fine thing to brag about, baker, but the text doesn't say it. Haman says, "Queen Esther invited no one but me to join the king at the banquet she prepared, and I am invited back tomorrow along with the king." (Esther 5:12) The brag is about the invitation.

You'd think so, friend, after a list that long. But Haman says, "Yet none of this satisfies me as long as I see Mordecai the Jew sitting at the king's gate." (Esther 5:13) The wealth, the sons and the banquet invitation still leave him unsatisfied. So the statement on the card is the false one.

That's right, baker. Haman says, "Yet none of this satisfies me as long as I see Mordecai the Jew sitting at the king's gate." (Esther 5:13) He just listed all that wealth and honor, and it still isn't enough for him. One man sitting at a gate is spoiling the whole batch for Haman.

That's what the text says, baker, and I think this one hurts. Zeresh, Haman's wife, and his friends tell him, "Have them build a gallows fifty cubits high, and ask the king in the morning to have Mordecai hanged on it." (Esther 5:14) It's a heavy verse. Mordecai is the one the plan is aimed at.

explanations.answer: A prison next to the gate
explanations.explanation: I understand the guess, friend, but that's not what the text says. Zeresh, Haman's wife, and his friends tell him, "Have them build a gallows fifty cubits high, and ask the king in the morning to have Mordecai hanged on it." (Esther 5:14) It's a heavy verse, and the gallows is what they ask for.

explanations.answer: A tower over the city wall
explanations.explanation: A tower is a big build, baker, but it's not in this verse. Zeresh, Haman's wife, and his friends tell him, "Have them build a gallows fifty cubits high, and ask the king in the morning to have Mordecai hanged on it." (Esther 5:14) It's a heavy verse, and what they name is a gallows.

That's right, friend. After the gallows advice, Zeresh and his friends add, "Then go to the banquet with the king and enjoy yourself." (Esther 5:14) They hand Haman the plan and tell him to enjoy the evening. The banquet is still on the calendar.

I see why you'd hesitate, baker, with the gallows advice in the same verse. But Zeresh and his friends do say, "Then go to the banquet with the king and enjoy yourself." (Esther 5:14) They tell him to build the gallows and still go enjoy himself. So the statement on the card is true.
